cards.front: In a traditional colon-style switch, can two cases each declare a local variable with the same name?
cards.back: No — that is a compile-time error: the whole switch block is one scope.
cards.extra: Both declarations land in the same scope, so int temp = 20; in case 2 collides with int temp = 10; in case 1 even though you mentally treat them as separate cases.
cards.example:
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        int temp = 10;
        break;
    case 2:
        int temp = 20;   // compile error: temp is already defined in the switch block
        break;
}

cards.front: Why can't a colon-style switch case safely reuse a variable declared in an earlier case?
cards.back: Control may jump straight to that case, so the earlier declaration never ran and the variable is uninitialised.
cards.extra: Case labels are jump targets, not sequential steps. Entering at case 2 skips int temp = 10; in case 1, so reading temp there fails with 'variable might not have been initialized'.
cards.example:
switch (day) {
    case 1:
        int temp = 10;
        break;
    case 2:
        // System.out.println(temp);  // compile error: temp may not have been initialized
        break;
}

cards.front: What scope does an arrow case body case L -> { ... } get in a switch expression?
cards.back: Its own block scope — the same local name may be redeclared in another case.
cards.extra: Each arrow body is a separate block, so variables declared inside it live only until its closing brace. That is what removes the name-collision problem of the colon form.
cards.example:
int result = switch (day) {
    case 1 -> {
        int temp = 10;   // local to case 1
        yield temp * 2;
    }
    case 2 -> {
        int temp = 20;   // valid: a different local variable
        yield temp * 3;
    }
    default -> 0;
};
